notes:
Task and constraints: Return every shortest word sequence from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter per step and using words from wordList; the output may contain several paths.
Idea: Build a set named words, then run level-by-level BFS from front. For each word, replace each character with a-z, record each valid candidate's predecessor in parents, and stop after finishing the first level that reaches endWord. build(endWord) walks parents backward using path and appends reversed paths to out.
Technique and why it applies: BFS finds the minimum number of transformations, while a predecessor graph preserves all same-depth routes needed to enumerate every shortest sequence.
Invariant: Before each BFS level, front contains words at one distance from beginWord; parents[v] records only words from the preceding level that can reach v by one letter change.
Edge cases: If endWord is absent from words, return []. A direct one-letter transformation produces a two-word path. Multiple parents at the first successful level must all be retained so both hit-hot-dot-dog-cog and hit-hot-lot-log-cog are returned.
Complexity: BFS tests 25 replacements per character per visited word, roughly O(W*L^2) with string construction; path reconstruction is output-sensitive. Memory is O(W*L) for words and parents plus stored output paths.
complexity_reason: BFS generates up to 25 replacement strings for each character of each visited word, and parents plus out store the predecessor graph and all shortest paths.

notes:
Task and constraints: Enumerate all shortest transformations between equal-length beginWord and endWord, using dictionary words and changing exactly one character at each edge.
Idea: findLadders initializes words, front, and parents, then repeatedly removes the current front from words and tries every lowercase replacement in a char array. It records each valid predecessor, completes the successful level, and calls build to reverse each parent chain into out.
Technique and why it applies: Layered breadth-first search establishes shortest distance first; a Map from each word to its prior-level words keeps ties rather than selecting only one route.
Invariant: At each iteration, front is one BFS depth, and parents entries point from a newly discovered word to words at the immediately preceding depth.
Edge cases: If endWord is not in wordList, the initially empty out is returned. A direct neighbor yields a path with two entries. The old character is restored after trying a position, preventing one candidate mutation from leaking into the next replacement.
Complexity: Replacement generation and string construction take about O(W*L^2) time for W words of length L; reconstruction depends on the number and lengths of output paths. Space is O(W*L) for words and parents, excluding output.
complexity_reason: The BFS performs up to 25 character substitutions per position for each visited word, and parents retains all shortest predecessor links.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the only integer occurring once when every other value occurs twice, using linear time and constant extra space.
Idea: singleNumber starts x at zero, XORs each array element v into x, and returns the accumulated result after the for-each loop.
Technique and why it applies: Bitwise XOR is associative and commutative, and x XOR x equals zero while x XOR zero equals x, so paired values cancel regardless of their positions.
Invariant: After processing each prefix of nums, x equals the XOR of all values in that prefix; completed duplicate pairs contribute no remaining bits.
Edge cases: A one-element array such as [1] returns 1. In [2,2,1], the two 2 values cancel and x remains 1. Negative Java int values also work because XOR operates on the fixed 32-bit representation, without arithmetic overflow concerns.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each nums element is visited once; auxiliary space is O(1) because only the integer x is maintained.
complexity_reason: The enhanced for loop visits each of n integers once and updates a single int variable x.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return every sentence that splits s into dictionary words; multiple valid segmentations can exist, so runtime depends on the number of sentences produced.
Idea: Convert wordDict to words and memoize build(i), which returns all valid sentence suffixes beginning at index i. The base case at len(s) returns a tuple containing the empty suffix. For each word matching s.startswith(word,i), prepend it to every suffix from build(i+len(word)).
Technique and why it applies: Memoized recursion over start indices avoids recomputing the same suffix segmentations while exploring each possible dictionary prefix.
Invariant: Each string returned by build(i) spells exactly s[i:] and uses only entries from words separated by single spaces.
Edge cases: If no dictionary word matches at i, build(i) returns an empty tuple. For catsanddog, the matches cats+and+dog and cat+sand+dog yield two sentences. The empty suffix base case lets a word ending at len(s) be emitted without a trailing space.
Complexity: The number of states is at most O(n), but combining and storing sentence lists is output-sensitive and exponential in the worst case; memoized suffix results and output consume corresponding space.
complexity_reason: Each cached build index tests every word in words and stores all sentence suffix combinations reachable from that index.

notes:
Task and constraints: Produce all space-separated dictionary segmentations of s, with output size potentially exponential as the number of valid sentences grows.
Idea: wordBreak stores s, words, and memo on the Solution instance and starts build(0). build(i) checks memo, tries every dictionary word whose prefix matches s at i, recursively obtains suffix sentences, and combines each with w before caching the list.
Technique and why it applies: Memoization keyed by the start index reuses suffix sentence lists across different prefix choices, while recursion enumerates each valid next word.
Invariant: Every entry cached under i is a complete valid segmentation of the suffix beginning at i; each recursive call advances by w.length(), so it cannot reuse the same prefix indefinitely.
Edge cases: If no word begins at i, out stays empty and is cached. When i equals s.length(), the method returns a list containing an empty string so the preceding word is not followed by an extra space. HashSet removes duplicate dictionary entries.
Complexity: There are O(n) memo indices, but sentence construction and storage are output-sensitive and exponential in the worst case; memo plus returned strings determine space use.
complexity_reason: build(i) tests the dictionary at each uncached suffix index and stores all concatenated sentence variants in memo.
